title: Prospective surveillance study of acute respiratory infections, influenza-like illness and seasonal influenza vaccine in a cohort of juvenile idiopathic arthritis patients.
ehr_evidence: Surveillance of respiratory viruses was conducted in JIA patients during ARI season in two consecutive years (2007 and 2008) at a tertiary Pediatric Rheumatology Clinic; nasopharyngeal swabs were collected for real-time PCR and serum was tested by hemagglutination inhibition, with medical records analyzed retrospectively to identify temporal associations between ARI/ILI episodes and disease worsening.
summary: A prospective longitudinal surveillance cohort study of children and adolescents with juvenile idiopathic arthritis evaluated the frequency of acute respiratory infections and influenza-like illness episodes, their temporal association with JIA flares, and the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent split influenza vaccine.
key_findings: ARI attack rate was 7.6 (95% CI 5.9-9.8) per 1000 child-days in SV1 and 3.9 (95% CI 2.8-5.5) in SV2, significantly more frequent in SV1 (p<0.01).
26.6% (28/105) of ARI episodes were classified as influenza-like illness.
60.6% (20/33) of nasopharyngeal samples were positive for at least one respiratory virus, with influenza and rhinovirus the most frequently detected (~30% each).
20% (10/50) of JIA flares or worsening episodes were temporally associated with ARI/ILI, more frequently in systemic-onset JIA (p=0.03).
Influenza seroprotection rates exceeded 70% (91-100%) and seroconversion rates exceeded 40% (74-93%).
Patients on anti-TNF alpha drugs had lower seroconversion to the H1N1 strain (p=0.03) and 60% seroprotection.
No significant difference in ACRPed30 before vs after vaccination (p=0.22), and no patient reported ILI during the 6-month post-vaccine follow-up.
captured_features: ARI episode counts and attack rate per 1000 child-days
Respiratory virus detection by real-time PCR (nasopharyngeal swabs)
Influenza hemagglutination inhibition antibody titers (GMT, seroprotection, seroconversion)
population: Children and adolescents with juvenile idiopathic arthritis attending a tertiary Pediatric Rheumatology Clinic in Brazil (mean age ~11 years), studied across two ARI seasons (2007 and 2008), with a healthy control group of 10 children vaccinated in 2008.
exposure_domain: Respiratory viral infections (acute respiratory infections/influenza-like illness) and influenza vaccination
limitations: Small sample size, limiting power for subgroup and adjusted analyses (e.g., anti-TNF response).
Retrospective chart review for temporal association cannot establish causality between ARI and JIA flares.
Single-center design with potential selection bias from loss to follow-up.
No unvaccinated comparison for ARI frequency and differing seasonality between surveillance periods limits vaccine effectiveness inference.
